prompt:
Extract a SysML v2 model from the document as a list of facts. Each fact has unit_id (the sentence it comes from), type and slots. Give only the slots that have a value, as a list of {slot, value} pairs; for composition give one 'parts' pair per part.

Types and slots:
  attribute(owner,name,value,unit) action(performer,label) state(owner,label) constraint(subject,expression) requirement(subject,text)
  composition(whole,parts) flow(source,target,payload) succession(before,after) transition(from,to,trigger) allocation(action,to)

Name each element by its full name as first introduced in the document.
RULES:
- Resolve every entity-valued slot using all the text you are given. If a sentence refers to an element by an alias, abbreviation, pronoun or shorter description, write the element's full name as first introduced. If a sentence says an element receives or uses an item and the text you are given states which element produces or sends that item, emit a flow from that producer to the receiver. If an element cannot be determined from the text you are given, use null; never guess.
- Never write placeholder words such as "any", "all", "some state" for an unstated element; use null.
- Do not merge differently named things unless the text says they are the same.
- Emit one action for EVERY behavior verb phrase, including passive voice (performer null), capability statements, displays, logs, generates and reports. label = the verbatim verb phrase with its object.
- Emit a requirement for every NORMATIVE statement (shall, must, should, will, is required to, needs to). Purpose, goal or benefit sentences are not requirements.
- Emit a state for every named mode or state; transitions use the state names, with from null when the prior state is not stated.
- Emit a succession only for an EXPLICIT temporal connective between two actions ("then", "after", "once", "before", "when ... is complete", "next", "finally"); before/after are the action labels. Never use succession for cause or data transfer.
- Resolve a pronoun or "this/these" performer to the element named in the preceding sentence and write that element's name; if it cannot be resolved, use null. Never output a pronoun as a slot value.
- Drop determiners and quantifiers from element names ("Each Soil Moisture Probe" -> "Soil Moisture Probe", "the system" -> "system").
- allocation.to must be a component or actor, never a mode or state.
- Emit a constraint for every threshold, limit, period or deadline stated with a number; expression = the verbatim phrase.
- Emit a flow for every sentence in which an element sends, transmits, reports, displays, commands or delivers an item (target null if the receiver is not named).
 Also list under "entities" every system element, actor or item named in the document units, with its full name and any alias the text explicitly declares for it (e.g. 'hereafter X', 'known as X', 'called X'); aliases [] if none. Return JSON {"entities": [...], "facts": [...]}.

Document units:
S133: Station status indications presented to local station staff are derived from validated CBTC states rather than from unverified field contacts alone.
S134: These indications distinguish normal service, held train, door interlock fault, radio degraded, emergency stop active, and evacuation support conditions.
S135: The Metro Operations Control System displays station and platform states with the same identifiers used in controller workstations to reduce interpretation errors during incidents.
S136: Passenger Information Gateway receives train prediction data, stopping pattern changes, and platform allocation updates after the CBTC system has reconciled them with the active timetable.
S137: The Passenger Information Gateway shall not publish a revised destination or skip-stop message until the underlying train identity and route have been confirmed by the CBTC system.
S138: When a platform is taken out of service, the passenger information interface marks the affected train movements as unavailable for boarding while retaining their operational tracking in the control center.
S139: Service Timetable Server provides planned service context used to compare predicted arrivals against scheduled platform usage.
S140: Metro Operations Control System coordinates timetable deviation, platform closure, and station crowding information before it is released to passenger-facing systems.
S141: Voice Dispatch Console displays train calling identity, current platform association, and the latest operational hold reason so that spoken instructions match automated indications.
S142: The Line Traffic Controller may apply a station hold through dispatch controls, and the hold is reflected in CBTC departure logic without changing the underlying route locking rules.
S143: Dispatch-related controls use positive confirmation and cancellation states so that a cancelled hold is not confused with a timeout, failed message, or rejected command.
S144: Kestrel shall report train door enable side, berth identity, and departure readiness to support platform interface checks during dwell and dispatch.
S145: Saffron shall maintain message delivery paths for station interface traffic during normal radio coverage transitions and degraded coverage recovery.
S146: Train Radio Modem uses the Encryption Certificate Renewal Pack before accepting renewed secure sessions for passenger-facing and station-interface data paths.
S147: Safety Data Communication Network carries safety-relevant station interface messages separately from nonvital passenger information messages.
S148: Maintenance Diagnostic Server records station interface faults, rejected commands, and inconsistent indications for later investigation by the Signal Maintenance Engineer.
S149: Cyber Security Officer reviews access rights for passenger information and dispatch integration workstations when station-facing interfaces are commissioned or materially changed.
S150: During degraded operation, the CBTC system favours restrictive platform states and requires explicit controller action before restoring automatic departure support at the affected station.
S151: Diagnostics and maintenance for the Greenvale Metro communications-based train control system are organised around prompt event collection, controlled remote access, and traceable engineering decisions.
S152: Each safety-related part records time-stamped events for state changes, command acceptance, rejected commands, communication loss, and local protective actions.
S153: The Maintenance Diagnostic Server receives event streams from fixed and onboard equipment through monitored interfaces that do not allow maintenance traffic to alter train movement authority.
S154: The Maintenance Diagnostic Server uses the checksum log to compare stored braking data identifiers against the expected maintenance baseline for the affected train.
S155: Remote diagnostic sessions are initiated by a Signal Maintenance Engineer and are limited to read-only observation unless an approved maintenance window authorises a specific intervention.
S156: The Cyber Security Officer reviews privileged diagnostic access logs and confirms that remote connections use current credentials and approved encryption settings.
S157: The Line Traffic Controller receives the Route Release Exception List during incident triage and uses it to check whether a release anomaly could affect service recovery decisions.
S158: Marble records controller health, interface state, and fallback mode transitions in a form that can be correlated with adjacent wayside and operations records.
S159: The South District Zone Controller maintains comparable diagnostic coverage so that boundary events can be reviewed without relying on a single source of evidence.
S160: The East Junction Interlocking and West Junction Interlocking report route command histories, point detection changes, and protective lock status to support failure localisation.
S161: The Atlas Onboard Controller stores onboard fault codes, movement authority acceptance records, propulsion cutback requests, and train interface exceptions for later retrieval.
S162: The Dual Channel Odometer provides distance and speed plausibility information that is retained with trainborne diagnostic records after any odometry disagreement.
S163: The Train Radio Modem records bearer loss, reconnection timing, signal quality indicators, and message retry counts needed to distinguish radio coverage issues from equipment faults.
S164: The Wayside Radio Access Network and Safety Data Communication Network provide communication performance records that are compared with controller logs during network-related investigations.
S165: The Metro Operations Control System displays selected fault summaries to the Line Traffic Controller but does not expose detailed maintenance commands at the traffic control workstation.
S166: A Revenue Train Operator reports observed cab indications, train handling effects, and passenger service impacts using the operational reporting channel defined for degraded service.
